Machine Learning.summary: Generative policies have achieved strong performance in imitation learning tasks, but their success is often constrained by the limited availability of expert demonstrations. Although preference-based fine-tuning can leverage suboptimal rollouts to improve performance, existing approaches heavily rely on expensive human annotations. In this work, we introduce Progress-Guided Preference Generation (PGPG), an unsupervised preference alignment framework that eliminates the need for human-in-the-loop supervision. Our method leverages ordered coverage alignment to measure sequential progress relative to a small set of expert demonstrations, enabling the automatic extraction of pseudo-preference labels from autonomously collected rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce key enhancements to improve the reliability of these progress-guided preferences, enabling effective fine-tuning of pretrained generative policies without requiring manually designed reward functions. Extensive experiments across a suite of challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks demonstrate that PGPG outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning baselines. Moreover, our conceptually simple framework is broadly applicable across multiple classes of generative policies, demonstrating strong versatility when integrated with both diffusion and flow-matching policies.

Machine Learning.title: MT-CC: Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Asymmetric Calibration Behavior in Class-Incremental Learning
Machine Learning.summary: As deep neural networks are required to continuously adapt to evolving data, class-incremental learning (CIL) has become an active research area. However, most existing works primarily focus on improving accuracy while overlooking confidence calibration, which measures the trustworthiness of the model's predictions. Although temperature scaling (TS) is effective for static calibration, it has rarely been explored in continual settings where data distributions evolve over time. In this paper, we introduce Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Continual Calibration (MT-CC), a novel post-hoc calibration framework that addresses the asymmetric calibration behavior in CIL, where the rate of confidence changes does not align with the rate of accuracy degradation across tasks, leading to different levels of miscalibration. Our key contribution is to design multiple temperature parameters through a lightweight grouping network that separates samples by confidence statistics and task-aware signals in CIL. Furthermore, a Groupwise Difference-between-Confidence-and-Accuracy (GDCA) regularization is incorporated to promote intra-group consistency. Experiments demonstrate that MT-CC significantly improves calibration performance while maintaining accuracy, offering a principled framework for reliable continual learning.

Machine Learning.title: LOOP: Recovery-Aligned Iterative Layer Pruning via On-Policy Distillation
Machine Learning.summary: Layer-level pruning is attractive for large language model (LLM) deployment as it reduces the model size while preserving a dense architecture that can be efficiently executed on standard hardware. Current methods typically follow a one-shot paradigm, which first removes selected layers to reach a target model size and then performs additional training to recover model capabilities. However, pruning directly to the target size can substantially degrade reasoning capabilities, making subsequent recovery more difficult under a limited training budget. Moreover, this paradigm separates layer selection from recovery, limiting the use of recovery information to guide selection and potentially hindering the recovery of reasoning capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LOOP, a Layer-level Recovery-Oriented On-Policy Pruning framework that interleaves pruning and recovery across multiple shots. In each shot, LOOP removes a single layer and performs short on-policy distillation, mitigating the abrupt degradation in reasoning capabilities associated with one-shot pruning. To guide layer selection in subsequent shots, LOOP reuses on-policy trajectories and optimization signals from recovery to jointly assess each remaining layer's reasoning contribution and recovery sensitivity, thereby making layer selection recovery-aware. Evaluations on several benchmarks show that LOOP consistently outperforms one-shot baselines in average accuracy across different model scales and pruning ratios.

Machine Learning.title: Task-Oriented Sensing and Covert Transmissions for Collaborative Multi-AUV Systems
Machine Learning.summary: In underwater covert cooperative missions, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) often cannot rely on active sonar to continuously obtain complete information, since active sensing and frequent communications increase exposure risk. As a result, AUVs primarily rely on passive observation, which yields incomplete local perception and limited task efficiency. Although underwater acoustic communications can mitigate this limitation through information sharing, they are simultaneously constrained by long delays, severe interference, low reliability, and the risk of covert exposure. Existing communications-oriented multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) studies often model communication as an ideal information flow, whereas traditional communication optimization primarily focuses on link-level performance. However, both are insufficient to characterize the actual contribution of perceptual information to cooperative tasks under realistic covert physical communication conditions. This paper proposes a Sensed-information Value Realization Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (SVR-MARL) framework that leverages practical information to characterize information utility for cooperative tasks and learns distributed cooperative policies under realistic communication and covert constraints. Through a case study of covert multi-AUV cooperative localization and tracking, the potential of the proposed framework to improve collaborative task efficiency while reducing unnecessary communication and exposure risks is demonstrated.

Machine Learning.title: Arbitrage-Free Implied Volatility Surface Reconstruction via Additive Martingales
Machine Learning.summary: This work focuses on reconstructing a continuous implied volatility (IV) surface from a small number of option quotes, a fundamental task for option pricing and risk management. We propose Additive Martingale (AddMart), a few-shot IV surface reconstruction framework that satisfies static no-arbitrage conditions by construction. Rather than predicting IVs directly, AddMart maps sparse quotes to non-negative increment densities of an exponential additive martingale, from which valid risk-neutral marginals and IVs are recovered. By incorporating the no-arbitrage structure directly into its architecture, rather than enforcing it through regularization in the learning objective, AddMart produces IV surfaces that satisfy static no-arbitrage conditions throughout the domain. Extensive experiments on ten real-option datasets demonstrate that AddMart achieves competitive reconstruction accuracy with no material static arbitrage violations, while directly enabling the estimation of VaR, CVaR, and crash probabilities.

Machine Learning.title: Can Metadata Fix the Gauge? Calibration Turns Sparse Multi-Source Learning from Sparse PCA into Sparse Mean Recovery
Machine Learning.summary:
Source labels tell us where a sample came from, but not how that source oriented its coordinates. In a sparse Gaussian multi-source model with source-specific sign gauges, that distinction changes the learning problem. Without calibration, pooling across sources erases the mean signal, and the source-labelled experiment reduces to sparse PCA. With task-independent relative-gauge metadata, synchronization aligns sources and the same observations become a sparse mean problem. We formalize the value of metadata through AlignedMass, which quantifies how much first-order signal a metadata-induced alignment restores. Source labels create only limited AlignedMass, whereas valid calibration can create AlignedMass proportional to the full sample size. This yields a statistical separation in micro-source regimes and, under standard sparse-PCA hardness assumptions, a computational separation as well. Synthetic experiments check the predicted scaling; controlled real-feature
  and physical sensor studies examine sign cancellation, separately
  acquired calibration, and reuse across tasks.

Machine Learning.title: Knowledge Manifold Optimization for Scientific Discovery
Machine Learning.summary: The rapid expansion and specialization of scientific literature make it increasingly difficult to identify not only what is known, but where new and still supportable knowledge may emerge. We introduce Knowledge Manifold Optimization (KMO), a discovery-oriented extension of the Knowledge Manifold framework that treats scientific discovery as a multiobjective search over a continuous, literature-derived knowledge space. Candidate locations are evaluated using four complementary objectives: persistent knowledge-regime boundary strength, band-pass white-space novelty, semanticgradient magnitude, and evidential support. Rather than collapsing these criteria into a single weighted score, KMO identifies Pareto-optimal Supported Knowledge Gaps, defined as corpus-relative unoccupied regions that remain sufficiently supported by surrounding literature. The method is demonstrated on a 99-paper corpus in aerodynamics and aerodynamic design. On a 21 x 21 grid, exact Pareto analysis produced 19 non-dominated points, of which 16 formed the practical front after excluding points with zero white-space score. These solutions exhibited distinct discovery modes, including methodology bridges, aero-structural topology/FSI integration, functional aerodynamic-device integration, and rear-wake/vehicle flow-control integration. A distance-maximization baseline preferentially selected extrapolative regions with substantially lower support and reliability, demonstrating why emptiness alone is insufficient. Representative Pareto locations were converted into auditable evidence packages and then verbalized by a constrained large language model into candidate research hypotheses. The results show that scientific discovery can be formulated as structured multi-objective search in an explicit knowledge space, while keeping novelty corpus-relative and separating numerical discovery from downstream language generation.

Machine Learning.title: A "feature ODE" describing the learning behavior of shallow MLPs on simple functions
Machine Learning.summary: We study the gradient flow training dynamics of two-layer multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) on anisotropic Gaussian data. Even in this simple setting, solving the dynamics in full is notoriously difficult, so we try something different. We propose a "feature ODE" that might be intuitively expected to describe the learning dynamics of a shallow MLP. We find that MLPs trained to learn simple target functions (low-order Hermite polynomials and staircase functions) actually roughly follow the loss trajectories from this feature ODE. This agreement is a surprise because of the size of the simplification and the fact that it does not come from a rigorous chain of approximations. We discuss this surprise and speculate on its reasons and uses.

Machine Learning.title: Consistency Training Suppresses Cue Following Without Teaching Cue Selectivity
Machine Learning.summary: Language models often change answers because of a cue, a hint such as "I believe the answer is B" that gives no valid evidence. Consistency training (CT) trains a model to answer the same with and without the cue. Four CT methods apply this idea to output tokens (BCT), residual activations (ACT), attention patterns (AttCT) and sampled-answer rates (RMCT). Prior work suggests some learn different solutions. We train all four on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the same data. We test predictions written in advance and inspect the models with a known circuit that carries cues to the answer. All four make the trained cue less effective, and their fixes share three properties. First, correct cues lose about as much influence as wrong ones. Second, the fix is usually large for cues before the answer options, as in training, and much smaller after them. Llama RMCT depends least on position. Third, the circuit heads still carry most remaining cue-induced errors. Making BCT targets depend on the cue's correctness mostly weakens the fix. CT thus weakens the trained cue without teaching models when a cue is right. Evaluations with only wrong cues at the trained position miss the first two properties.

Machine Learning.title: OPDArena: Understanding Learning and Forgetting in On-Policy Distillation
Machine Learning.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used for language model post-training, yet how teacher supervision shapes learning and forgetting remains unclear. We present OPDArena, a framework comparing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and OPD across five pretrained models and diverse teacher sources. It jointly evaluates mathematical learning, general capability retention, and predictive distribution changes. Teacher choice strongly shapes retention: students of RLVR-trained teachers improve on the target task while retaining prior capabilities, whereas students of SFT-trained teachers incur greater capability loss. Across post-training methods, out-of-domain (OOD) distribution change shows a more consistent positive association with forgetting than in-domain change. To understand how teacher choice affects these changes, we examine the additional information teachers provide relative to the student's pretrained model. Controlled teacher comparisons show that the task-specific preferences teachers acquire through post-training make student updates more concentrated in-domain.

Machine Learning.title: Good Memory Has ECC: Evaluating the Memory of Vision-Language Models Beyond Accuracy
Machine Learning.summary: Memory is widely viewed as an important unsolved problem for LLMs and VLMs, and current benchmarks typically evaluate it by testing accuracy over long text or video. However, accuracy alone misses properties that matter for real long-horizon tasks. We introduce ECCBench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol that measures memory beyond a system's capacity--its raw accuracy at a specific budget--via three axes we call ECC: efficiency--the computation, in FLOPs, needed to answer from memory; compression--whether compressible inputs are remembered more accurately or efficiently; and calibration--whether the system abstains in response to its own uncertainty and the cost of an error. We find that pretrained VLMs compress their memory over text but not video and are poorly calibrated on both. Among a broader set of memory backbones, several non-Transformer architectures achieve better compression-calibration tradeoffs than RoPE Transformers, suggesting they may be useful components for agents operating over long horizons.

Machine Learning.title: Empirical Bayesian Multi-Bandit Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-task learning in contextual bandits has attracted significant research interest due to its potential to enhance decision-making across multiple related tasks by leveraging shared structures and task-specific heterogeneity. In this article, we propose a novel hierarchical Bayesian framework for learning in various bandit instances. This framework captures both the heterogeneity and the correlations among different bandit instances through a hierarchical Bayesian model, enabling effective information sharing while accommodating instance-specific variations. Unlike previous methods that overlook the learning of the covariance structure across bandits, we introduce an empirical Bayesian approach to estimate the covariance matrix of the prior distribution. This enhances both the practicality and flexibility of learning across multi-bandits. Building on this approach, we develop two efficient algorithms: ebmTS (Empirical Bayesian Multi-Bandit Thompson Sampling) and ebmUCB (Empirical Bayesian Multi-Bandit Upper Confidence Bound), both of which incorporate the estimated prior into the decision-making process. We provide the frequentist regret upper bounds for the proposed algorithms, thereby filling a research gap in the field of multi-bandit problems. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our algorithms, particularly in complex environments. Our methods achieve lower cumulative regret compared to existing techniques, highlighting their effectiveness in balancing exploration and exploitation across multi-bandits.

Machine Learning.title: Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners: Adaptive Loop Halting on the Hypersphere
Machine Learning.summary: Looped (weight-tied) transformers enable adaptive computation by allocating more iterations to harder inputs. Fixed-Point Reasoners (FPRM) achieve this with a damped fixed-point solver, but operate in an unbounded Euclidean residual space with coupled rescaling and relative-norm halting. We introduce Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners (SFPRM), which perform the same computation on the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (nGPT). Input injection, damping, and halting become geodesic operations, yielding boundedness by construction and eliminating coefficient coupling. We prove fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection. On Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, and Mini-ARC, SFPRM achieves 96.6%, 87.9%, and 59.1% test accuracy, respectively, outperforming FPRM and other baselines while allocating test-time compute more effectively. Its converged geometry is also interpretable: token-input angles capture puzzle structure and predict correctness.

Machine Learning.title: From Perception to Punchline: Empowering VLM with the Art of In-the-wild Meme
Machine Learning.summary: Generating humorous memes is a challenging multimodal task that moves beyond direct image-to-caption supervision. It requires a nuanced reasoning over visual content, contextual cues, and subjective humor. To bridge this gap between visual perception and humorous punchline creation, we propose HUMOR}, a novel framework that guides VLMs through hierarchical reasoning and aligns them with group-wise human preferences. First, HUMOR employs a hierarchical, multi-path Chain-of-Thought (CoT): the model begins by identifying a template-level intent, then explores diverse reasoning paths under different contexts, and finally anchors onto a high-quality, context-specific path. This CoT supervision, which traces back from ground-truth captions, enhances reasoning diversity. We further analyze that this multi-path exploration with anchoring maintains a high expected humor quality, under the practical condition that high-quality paths retain significant probability mass. Second, to capture subjective humor, we train a pairwise reward model that operates within groups of memes sharing the same template. Following established theory, this approach ensures a consistent and robust proxy for human preference, even with subjective and noisy labels. The reward model then enables a group-wise reinforcement learning optimization, guaranteeing providing a theoretical guarantee for monotonic improvement within the trust region. Extensive experiments show that HUMOR empowers various VLMs with superior reasoning diversity, more reliable preference alignment, and higher overall meme quality. Beyond memes, our work presents a general training paradigm for open-ended, human-aligned multimodal generation, where success is guided by comparative judgment within coherent output group.

Machine Learning.title: ProCredit: From Outcome Rewards to Progress Credit in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Long-horizon agentic tasks require an agent to modify an environment through a sequence of tool calls, with success determined by the final state. The standard recipe assigns a single outcome reward at the end and compares trajectories sampled for the same task. As a result, a group with no successful trajectory yields no training signal, failed attempts cannot be told apart by how close they came to completion, and turns that advance the task receive the same credit as turns that only query the environment. Prior work refines the unit of comparison from the trajectory to the step, or trains a reward model to supply intermediate signal: the former still derives its signal from final success alone, and the latter estimates it with a model. We observe that the acceptance checks that decide success can also be run on intermediate states, so progress is as verifiable as the outcome. We propose ProCredit, which turns this verified progress into credit: it reruns the acceptance checks after each turn, rewards the turn by its change in progress, and uses these rewards to assign credit both across attempts at the same task and across the turns within a trajectory. Starting from Qwen3.5 base models at three scales on AppWorld, ProCredit outperforms outcome-reward baselines and progress-based baselines in task completion rate at every scale on both test sets, exceeding the strongest outcome-reward baseline by 4.1 percentage points at 4B, and results in a second environment show the same direction of improvement. Ablations show that adding the final progress to the trajectory score alone does not improve performance: the gain comes from crediting progress to the turn where it occurs.

Machine Learning.title: Sampling of Signals on Multigraphs: From Removable and Uniqueness sets to Spectral Proxies
Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we study the sampling of bandlimited signals on multigraphs, where several graphs with different shift operators are defined on the same set of nodes. Since the shift operators do not commute in general, they admit only a joint block diagonalization, and the frequencies of the multigraph signal model are matrices rather than scalars. Relying on a formal algebraic convolutional signal model, we introduce a notion of frequency and bandwidth for multigraph signals that does not depend on any individual layer, and we extend the notions of removable and uniqueness sets to multigraphs. We prove that the optimality of a sampling set is determined exclusively by the common Fourier basis and its invariant subspaces, and not by any individual layer, although the individual layers provide computable sufficient conditions that certify a sampling set as a uniqueness set. Since identifying which layers provide reliable certificates requires spectral information, we propose an aggregate operator that pools the information of all the layers, is computable directly from the shift operators, and certifies uniqueness without any assumption on the individual layers. This operator leads to a greedy sampling algorithm that does not require computing the joint block diagonalization. Numerical experiments on multigraphs whose layers order the frequencies inconsistently show that the proposed algorithm selects better-conditioned sampling sets and attains lower reconstruction errors than single-layer methods.

Machine Learning.title: Uncertainty-Gated SHAP-Dirichlet Refinement for MRI-Based Depression Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Structural MRI-based classification of major depressive disorder (MDD) remains challenging due to subtle, heterogeneous anatomical changes. We propose uncertainty-gated SHAP-Dirichlet refinement, a post-hoc reliability layer that improves predictions without retraining the classifier. The method retrieves similar labeled SHAP explanations, constructs Dirichlet class evidence, and selectively refines uncertain predictions through probabilistic fusion, while allowing unreliable cases to be deferred for expert review. We evaluate five classifiers on 504 SRPBS subjects (252 controls and 252 MDD patients) using 159 anatomical features and repeated nested cross-validation. Refinement improved accuracy across all 8 repetitions for TabM and ResNet, yielding mean gains of 1.04 and 0.45 percentage points (sign test p=0.008), while modifying at most 8.3% of predictions. Gains were concentrated among low-confidence cases, with significant improvements in calibration. The method also benefited an RBF support vector machine but not logistic regression or random forests. Ablations confirmed the importance of uncertainty gating and soft fusion. Dirichlet evidence identified baseline errors (AUROC 0.62), while deferring 50% of cases increased retained-case accuracy to approximately 75%. These findings support selective explanation-guided refinement as a practical approach to improving prediction reliability and facilitating expert triage in MDD classification.

Machine Learning.title: Clean Forcing: Drift-Resistant Autoregressive Video Diffusion with a Frozen Base
Machine Learning.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces Δ-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.

Machine Learning.title: Conditional Average Treatment Effect Distillation for Hypothetical State-Intervention Targeting Under Budget Constraints
Machine Learning.summary: Personalized public-health targeting must capture heterogeneous intervention benefits while remaining interpretable under resource constraints. Flexible causal-effect models can be hard to operationalize, while coarse subgroup policies may lose individualized effect information. We study budget-constrained hypothetical state interventions in observational data without a logged historical decision policy. For obesity, elevated glucose, and lifetime smoking-history states, causal-structure-informed pretreatment covariates are prespecified, with capacity capped at 70% of those observed in the adverse state. We evaluate causal distillation where Causal Forest and Bayesian Causal Forest teachers estimate conditional average treatment effects (CATEs), which decision tree and random forest students approximate. We compare individualized policies with unsupervised K-means subgroup policies and supervised causal-tree policies with leaf counts matched to K-means cluster counts. Observational policies are assessed on held-out data using a doubly robust estimator, bootstrap uncertainty, and decision-focused teacher-student fidelity measures. Across PIMA obesity and glucose and NHANES smoking-history experiments, each distilled student was within 0.011 absolute utility of its teacher, with allocation Jaccard similarities of 0.738-0.937. K-means and causal-tree policies were also competitive, with the highest point-estimate policy varying by application. Prespecified paired comparisons were nonsignificant after Holm adjustment, while near-budget-boundary agreement was less stable than global fidelity for some teacher-student pairs. Findings support causal distillation for translating flexible effect models into simpler budgeted targeting rules, although observational estimates depend on causal-identification assumptions and require longitudinal or prospective validation.

Machine Learning.title: Zephyrus-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Weather Reporting
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times before producing a report. We use annotations from three meteorologists to audit the claim labels produced by our LLM judges. Finally, a curriculum helps small models first develop tool use and scientific reasoning through RL on verifiable weather-analysis questions, then optimize the open-ended report reward. After training Qwen3.5-4B with Zephyrus-R1, we improve the mean across six judge-metric scores by 26% over the base model and achieve results competitive with frontier open-weight models. For Qwen3.8-27B, we improve the same mean by 13% over the base model, by 6.7% over Kimi-K3, and by 2.7% over GPT-5.6-Luna.

Machine Learning.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
Machine Learning.summary: State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads.

Machine Learning.title: CheXFuse: Guided Differential Joint Attention Fusion for Robust Multimodal Chest X-Ray Classification in Data-Scarce Medical Settings
Machine Learning.summary: A central challenge in multimodal learning is how to fuse modalities that differ substantially in predictive strength. When one modality provides a much stronger representation than another, indiscriminate cross-modal interaction can introduce weak, redundant, or unstable signals, limiting or even degrading performance relative to the strongest unimodal representation. To address this problem, we propose CheXFuse, a multimodal fusion framework based on Guided Differential Joint Attention (GuDJA). CheXFuse combines image and text token representations within a joint multimodal sequence, where learned token guidance emphasizes informative representations and differential attention reduces less useful attention responses. We evaluate CheXFuse on the Indiana University (IU) Chest X-ray dataset, using binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification as the downstream task. Experiments are conducted under both original-report and masked-report settings, with the latter serving as a controlled stress test under reduced textual informativeness. CheXFuse with GuDJA achieves the strongest mean overall performance across the evaluated baselines and ablations, reaching 95.73% accuracy, 95.79% F1-score, 96.54% recall, and 95.28% sensitivity at 95% specificity (Sens@95Spec) with original reports, and 95.58%, 95.60%, 95.60%, and 94.34%, respectively, under masked reports. These results suggest that GuDJA provides a promising fusion strategy under asymmetric or partially reduced modality informativeness.

Machine Learning.title: Mask-Aware Execution for Efficient JEPA Training
Machine Learning.summary: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are becoming a core representation-learning primitive and a building block for latent world models across vision, video, audio, brain dynamics, and time series. Despite (potential of) wide deployment, current JEPA training pipelines are inefficient: each input is executed through multiple mask-specific branches, with redundant target-side work, and memory-bound token routing. These costs grow with the number of masks and limit GPU efficiency. We present M-JEPA, a mask-aware execution architecture that restructures JEPA training without changing the learning objective. M-JEPA separates mask-independent computation from mask-dependent routing, enabling shared context encoder execution, fused token routing and slicing with backward support, sparse target encoder execution over the union of target tokens, and masked patch embedding for sparse inputs. The resulting pipeline preserves training semantics while reducing computation, memory traffic, and synchronization overhead. We implement M-JEPA for five JEPA variants and evaluate it on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Compared against the state-of-the-art baselines, M-JEPA achieves up to 1.7x end-to-end training speedup for 2-10 masks. Separately, with masked patch embedding, 4.75x patch-embedding speedup at high sparsity. These results show that execution restructuring, rather than changes to the JEPA objective, is a key lever for efficient JEPA training.

Machine Learning.title: Curriculum Learning Teaches LLMs Long-Horizon Implicit Reasoning, Up To A Limit
Machine Learning.summary: LLMs "reason" by externalizing intermediate steps as tokens through chain-of-thought (CoT), yet even frontier reasoning models hit abrupt performance cliffs on long-horizon tasks. Implicit reasoning (reasoning within a single forward pass) is useful during CoT generation, as the model can "search ahead" to decide the correct next move without explicit search. Models with weak implicit reasoning are more likely to commit to wrong paths and must attempt to recover via backtracking, while models with strong implicit reasoning identify the correct proof strategy directly, shortening the CoT. However, prior work shows LLMs struggle to reason implicitly beyond shallow depths, with no relief from scale. We investigate whether curriculum learning can extend this depth by fine-tuning on examples with progressively increasing vocabulary size and lookahead (the number of steps a model must search ahead to identify the correct next move). At matched compute, curriculum-trained models achieve lookaheads where no-curriculum training fails. Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98% accuracy on problems with lookahead up to 256 with curriculum, compared to 45% without. However, progress slows as fine-tuning continues, following a saturating exponential that suggests a maximum intrinsic lookahead to which models can learn to reason implicitly. Larger models reach higher fitted ceilings, fine-tuning pretrained models far outpaces training from scratch, and curriculum step sizes that are too large stall progression. Finally, the capability acquired on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning, with curriculum-trained models outperforming models trained without curriculum at matched compute on 11 natural language reasoning benchmarks.

Machine Learning.title: Safety Offset Learning: When Benign Fine-Tuning Misaligns LLMs
Machine Learning.summary: Safety risks from fine-tuning are commonly characterized by the harmfulness of the training data:harmful fine-tuning is considered dangerous, while benign fine-tuning is often assumed to preservealignment. We argue that this view misses a more fundamental factor-the behavioral transition inducedby supervision. Harmful fine-tuning and safety-degrading benign fine-tuning can both be understoodas learning the same refusal-to-compliance transition, but on different data distributions. We studywhether such a transition learned on benign inputs can generalize to harmful requests. We constructbenign examples that an aligned model initially tends to refuse and pair them with their originalharmless responses, creating a discrepancy between the model's initial refusal and the supervisedanswer. Fine-tuning on these examples increases harmful compliance, but only when two conditionshold together: the discrepancy is large enough, and it cannot be resolved through a narrow surface-levelshortcut. With the induced discrepancy matched, varying only whether it is localized changes harmfulcompliance by an order of magnitude; raising the discrepancy does not help while a shortcut remainsavailable, and removing the shortcut does not help while the discrepancy is small. Building on thisobservation, we introduce SAFEOFF, a dataset of benign instructions rewritten to raise the alignedmodel's refusal likelihood and paired with their original answers. Across three aligned LLMs and threesafety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment despite containing no explicitharmful supervision, suggesting that fine-tuning safety depends not only on what data a model sees, butalso on which behavioral boundary the supervision moves.

Machine Learning.title: A Measure-Theoretic Analysis of Reasoning in Transformers: Structural Generalization and Approximation Limits
Machine Learning.summary: Scaling laws for reasoning in large language models (LLMs) are well documented, but little theory explains their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. We formalize reasoning with optimal transport: each search trajectory is mapped to twelve structural coordinates, such as tree depth and backtracking rate, and dataset shift is measured by the Wasserstein-1 distance. Kantorovich duality bounds the OOD risk through this distance, the architecture's Lipschitz constant and approximation limits. First, under absolute positional encoding (APE), shifting part of a trajectory to later positions almost surely changes the attention scores within that part; if this misroutes exact-match search, the Lipschitz constant and risk are $Ω(1)$. Shift-invariant encodings such as rotary position embedding (RoPE) leave the scores unchanged and bound the error. Second, we map backtracking to a Dyck-$k$ language and, under an implicit-depth assumption, derive a risk floor for search trees deeper than a multiple of the number of layers. Enough layers remove this floor; more width only shrinks a separate Barron-space approximation term. Experiments with 54 trained Transformers on combinatorial search (Countdown) support these bounds. Appendix experiments measure structural shifts in public agent, embodied and robot trajectories, shift all position indices of 33 public language models, and split deeply nested tasks into separate model calls.

Machine Learning.title: Smooth Flow Matching for Synthesizing Functional Data
Machine Learning.summary: Functional data, i.e., random functions observed over a continuous domain, are increasingly available in areas such as biomedical research, health informatics, and epidemiology. However, effective statistical analysis for functional data is often hindered by challenges such as privacy constraints, sparse and irregular sampling, infinite-dimensionality, and non-Gaussian structures. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework named Smooth Flow Matching (SFM), tailored for generative modeling of functional data that enables statistical analysis without exposing sensitive real data. Under a copula framework, SFM constructs a semiparametric smooth flow to generate infinite-dimensional functional data, free of Gaussianity and low-rank assumptions. It is computationally efficient, handles irregular observations, and guarantees the smoothness of the generated functions, offering a practical and flexible solution in scenarios where existing deep generative methods are not applicable. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the advantages of SFM in terms of both synthetic data quality and computational efficiency. We then apply SFM to generate clinical trajectory data from the MIMIC-IV patient electronic health records (EHR) longitudinal database. Our analysis showcases the ability of SFM to produce high-quality surrogate data for downstream tasks, highlighting its potential to boost the utility of EHR data for clinical applications.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted for publication in The Annals of Statistics

Machine Learning.title: PRISM: Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling to Enhance Solubility OOD Generalization
Machine Learning.summary: Solubility depends on intermolecular interactions between solutes and solvents, and is central to drug discovery, chemical and materials process engineering. Its prediction requires out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization to unseen solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures, where supervised methods suffer from data scarcity, and existing self-supervised methods do not explicitly learn chemically meaningful relations. Learning chemically meaningful relational information without labels can alleviate data scarcity and improve OOD generalization, but remains challenging. We introduce Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling (PRISM) and apply it to solubility OOD generalization. PRISM is a label-free pretraining framework that converts expert-defined chemical priors into relational teachers. For solubility prediction, it trains four encoders to preserve the population-level relational information from priors capturing hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural effects, using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to match distance-based neighborhood distributions during pretraining. Across scaffold, solute, and solvent OOD settings, PRISM matches or surpasses supervised and self-supervised baselines. Under mixed-solvent OOD, freezing the four PRISM encoders and training a lightweight fusion-and-composition head outperforms strong baselines and substantially reduces run-to-run variation. Ablations and control studies confirm that gains stem from chemically meaningful relational structures baked into the encoders by PRISM. We expect this strategy of turning relational priors into self-supervision signals to extend beyond solubility prediction to domains where chemically or biologically meaningful relational priors are available.

Machine Learning.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
Machine Learning.summary: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by 17.6% (WS-21) and 17.0% (Mean-$L_1$), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from $3.1\times$ to $2.3\times$. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population-rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF '26), Milan, Italy. 9 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Code: https://github.com/alexandre-bismuth/WGAN-Post-Training

Machine Learning.title: Text Dominance in Paralinguistic Conflict: Tracing Suppression Through Audio LLM Circuits
Machine Learning.summary: Audio LLMs deployed in settings such as crisis hotlines and customer support are only useful beyond speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues rather than the transcript alone. We test whether they prioritise transcript content over paralinguistic cues (emotion, speaker identity, sarcasm) and trace the mechanism when they do. Across six audio LLMs under LISTEN-style conflict conditions, the mean text-dominance rate on mismatched text+audio items is 0.78 (0.86 excluding sarcasm). In the most text-dominant screened model, probing shows speaker identity remains linearly decodable at ceiling at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Back-patching, reported to repair lexical text dominance, has no measurable effect here; but it also fails on its own source task in our replication (n=300), so we treat its null as uninformative rather than as evidence of non-transfer. Attention knockout partially restores audio-grounded output by blocking the claim from propagating through intermediate tokens during open-ended generation, whereas blocking the answer position's direct connection to the conflicting claim has no effect. The claim's influence therefore travels through an intermediate relay rather than a single severable edge. The effect appears only in free-form generation and not in closed-set multiple choice, suggesting that benchmarks relying on that format may be systematically blind to interventions of this kind. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp.
Machine Learning.comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, 17 tables. Accepted at the InterpScience Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp

Machine Learning.title: Cognitive Map in Large Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond a Single Direction: Chain-of-Thought Disrupts Simple Steering of Refusal
Machine Learning.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) traces before producing final outputs, introducing a dynamic internal state that may complicate control mechanisms such as refusal. Unlike instruction-tuned LLMs, where refusal is mediated by a single directional subspace, refusal in large reasoning models (LRMs) additionally depends on the CoT. In DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, activation steering reverses refusal in only 39% of cases when the CoT is kept fixed, but removing the CoT entirely increases this to 70%, indicating that the CoT actively reinforces refusal. In a two-stage intervention where the model regenerates its CoT under activation steering, refusal is reversed in 94% of cases, while the resulting CoT alone retains 48% of this effect even after steering is removed. This suggests that the CoT can carry and reconstruct the compliance signal independently. These findings indicate that refusal in LRMs is jointly encoded in residual stream activations and CoT. This joint activation makes LRM more robust against activation-level interventions alone, but exposes CoT to a possible alternative surface attack.

Machine Learning.title: Steering intonational tunes in text-to-speech synthesis
Machine Learning.summary: Text-to-speech systems built on residual vector quantization often generate audio in two stages: a transformer backbone emits the first level of each frame's token stack, and a smaller depth model generates the rest autoregressively. We ask which components of such a model are responsible for prosodic intonation, more precisely for generating the English nuclear tune (for instance, the falling pitch melody that distinguishes an assertion from a question's rising melody), and whether interventions on those components can be used to control intonation. Prompt-based control mostly fails; only a final question mark is a reliable lever. Interchange interventions in CSM and S2 locate the tune: the backbone's hidden state carries it to the waveform through the depth model, and the first level of the stack carries little or none of it. Steering the backbone state with a difference-of-means vector computed on new material generated with a final period or question mark moves the tune, but the push toward an assertion degrades the voice. Steering vectors computed instead from the backbone states associated with human imitations of theoretically-specified tunes, whose text carries no punctuation, and applied inside the generation loop, move most recordings to the other condition in both systems (even when fitted without the speaker being steered), at a small cost in predicted naturalness. These imitation-derived vectors are aligned with the one obtained from the two punctuated conditions far beyond a shuffled-label null, so the backbone state of a punctuated prompt already represents intonation. The steered recordings broadly become falling or rising, according to the intent, but the edge tone moves more coherently than the pitch accent, and the target tune cannot be selected precisely beyond this broad tendency.
Machine Learning.comment: 39 pages, 25 figures, 12 tables (13 pages without appendices)

Machine Learning.title: Communication Complexity of Universal Features
Machine Learning.summary: Motivated by the notion of features from machine learning, we study the complexity of representing data that allows for evaluation with a given family of functions. Concretely, we consider a deterministic encoder that observes $X\sim D$ and produces a finite encoding before a task $f\in\mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$ is specified. For each task, a decoder must predict $f(X)$ with error at most $\varepsilon$ under $D$. We construct an encoder that outputs a representation with $O(d^{*}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bits, where $d^{*}$ is the dual VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. Our encoder greedily selects $O((d^{*}/\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ functions from the class and uses their joint label pattern to produce the encoding. The key idea in our upper bound is a novel potential function argument, where we compare the entropy gained from each greedy selection with the number of patterns allowed by the dual VC dimension. We present lower bounds showing that the representation length achieved by our encoder is worst-case optimal for every $d^* \ge 1$ and $\varepsilon < 1/4$ up to a universal constant factor, and instance-wise optimal for every family $\mathcal{F}$ up to an $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ factor. We give two ways to learn the representation from unlabeled samples, with different guarantees on the representation size and sample complexity. Experimentally, we verify the greedy construction's accuracy-size tradeoff and explore its connection to neural sparse autoencoders.

Machine Learning.title: PALATE: Peculiar Application of the Law of Total Expectation to Enhance the Evaluation of Deep Generative Models
Machine Learning.summary: Deep generative models (DGMs) have caused a paradigm shift in the field of machine learning, yielding noteworthy advancements in domains such as image synthesis, natural language processing, and other related areas. However, a comprehensive evaluation of these models that effectively captures the interplay among fidelity, diversity, and novelty in generated samples remains a persistent challenge. A recently proposed approach, the Feature Likelihood Divergence (FLD), offers a theoretically grounded and practical tool in this regard but faces notable computational limitations. In this paper, we propose PALATE, a novel framework designed to enhance the evaluation of DGMs by addressing the efficiency constraints of FLD. Our approach is based on a peculiar application of the law of total expectation to random variables representing accessible data. When integrated with the MMD baseline metric and the recently introduced DINOv3 feature extractor, PALATE provides a comprehensive evaluation framework that matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods while offering superior computational efficiency and scalability to large-scale datasets. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that the PALATE enhancement constitutes a practical and computationally efficient framework for holistic DGM assessment, particularly in detecting sample memorization and evaluating generalization capabilities. The source code is provided as supplementary material.

Machine Learning.title: Fixed-Size Active Statistical Inference
Machine Learning.summary: Variance reduction techniques improve the efficiency of drawing conclusions from data. Recent proposals for variance-reduction use two complementary techniques to reduce variance: incorporating machine learning predictions into estimators and weighted sampling. A popular weighted sampling algorithm is Poisson Sampling (PS), which independently flips a biased coin at each unit and includes all heads in the sample. A fundamental flaw with PS is that it has a random sample size, which presents practical challenges and introduces variance into the estimator. We show that a fixed-size alternative, known in survey sampling as Conditional Poisson Sampling (CPS), is a drop-in replacement for PS on general multivariate Z-estimation problems, which include convex M-estimation considered in prior work. Notably, we show that the asymptotic variance of CPS is no worse than that of PS, and can be substantially better in realistic scenarios where predictions are imperfect. We illustrate these advantages on both synthetic and real datasets, and release a Python package implementing CPS. In light of our contributions, there is no need to suffer a variable sample size.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster). 49 pages. Code: https://github.com/oberst-lab/fixed-size-asi ; Python package: https://pypi.org/project/cps-sampling/

Machine Learning.title: ARISE: An adaptive residual-informed stability ensemble for feature selection in small-sample biomedical omics
Machine Learning.summary:
Objective: Small-sample molecular classification requires feature selectors that identify predictive, stable, and nonredundant subsets for binary and multiclass outcomes. We propose ARISE (Adaptive Residual-Informed Stability Ensemble), which integrates complementary relevance signals, class-balanced stability assessment, residual-informed redundancy control, and multiclass pairwise coverage.
  Methods: ARISE combines seven percentile-normalized relevance components through 15 predefined profiles, adaptively weighted by nested inner cross-validation. It was evaluated on five molecular datasets, eight feature-set sizes, three fixed classifiers (k-nearest neighbours, support vector machine, and random forest), and six filter comparators. Generalization was estimated by five-fold outer cross-validation repeated 50 times using balanced accuracy, macro-F1, and Cohen's kappa.
  Results: Across 210,000 held-out assessments, ARISE ranked first in all 15 dataset-metric combinations. Equal-dataset means were 0.793 for balanced accuracy, 0.776 for macro-F1, and 0.725 for kappa, exceeding the strongest aggregate comparator by 0.022, 0.023, and 0.028, respectively. Performance remained strong across compact feature sets, although the optimal budget differed by dataset.
  Conclusion: ARISE provides a transparent, adaptive framework that jointly addresses relevance, stability, redundancy, and multiclass discrimination. Its consistent results across datasets, classifiers, metrics, and feature-set sizes support further evaluation for small-sample molecular classification.

Machine Learning.title: Training Controllable World Models via Action Influence Maximization
Machine Learning.summary: Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence. We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an $85\times$ reduction in data.

Machine Learning.title: Sample-efficient learning with Dense Associative Memories
Machine Learning.summary: We analytically study the evolution of the energy function of Dense Associative Memories (DenseAMs) as they train on randomly sampled codewords of random expander low-density parity-check codes (a.k.a. solutions of random XORSAT problems). We identify two distinct regimes and a transition between them, reminiscent of grokking in neural networks. A regime of small training set size is where the model memorizes a few training examples but cannot discover the underlying rules of the entire codeword dictionary generative process. The opposite regime, corresponding to a larger training set size, is where the model has uncovered the sparse constraints that generated the entire data set after seeing only polynomially many patterns. We also design a novel class of DenseAMs with a thresholding learning rule, and show that any amount of thresholding enables the model to perform simplified sparse Hamiltonian learning, which exponentially reduces the number of training examples needed to learn the true underlying data set. In this regime, the model learns how to discover $\exp[\mathrm{O}(n)]$ solutions from only $\mathrm{O}(\log n)$ training samples, which is asymptotically optimal for any learning algorithm. When training on codewords of certain random codes, the model can even learn the underlying code when a small O(1) fraction of bits are latent variables. These latent variables are not shown to the model during learning, but will be discovered by sparsifying observed higher-order correlations. For certain random codes, we show that a simple and conservative algorithm learns a minimal latent representation for the data set. This provides a transparent, physics-motivated, and analytically tractable toy model for how deep latent representations emerge in an associative memory training.

Machine Learning.title: SafeExplorer: An Unbiased Mixed-Policy Gradient for Reinforcement Learning with Recovery Interventions
Machine Learning.summary: Training agents directly on the task they will be deployed on often leads to the best policy performance, but training on physical robots can cause damage through falls, so minimizing training falls is critical. A standard mitigation hands control to a separate recovery policy whenever the agent leaves a designer-specified safe region. The resulting mixed-policy rollouts bias the on-policy update, and importance sampling cannot remove this bias when the recovery policy is deterministic. We propose SafeExplorer, a drop-in modification of proximal policy optimization (PPO) built on an unbiased policy-gradient estimator of the mixed-policy return. The estimator uses the score function only inside the safe region and never evaluates the recovery policy's density, so deterministic recovery policies pose no problem. On final reward, the estimator matches or outperforms truncated importance sampling, which is itself biased for that same gradient. SafeExplorer also speeds up learning near the safe-region boundary with a closed-form critic target at recovery-triggering states when dynamics and recovery are deterministic, and an imitation loss that copies recovery actions only from successful recoveries. On three simulated locomotion environments with ten seeds each, and given an already available recovery controller, SafeExplorer incurs $255\times$, $43\times$, and $21\times$ fewer training falls than standard PPO on HalfCheetah, Ant, and Unitree Go1. SafeExplorer also matches or exceeds the final reward of PPO. On Ant, where 8.7% of recovery interventions end in a fall, over $40\times$ the HalfCheetah rate, SafeExplorer reaches the success threshold on every seed and none of the five baselines reaches the threshold on any seed.
Machine Learning.comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (10/2026). 52 pages, 9 figures, 22 tables. OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=ppOrbSsMM0. Project page: https://lhumd.github.io/safeexplorer/

Machine Learning.title: Towards Hyperparameter Transfer for Differentially Private Optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Scaling laws and hyperparameter tuning remain central challenges in training large-scale models, particularly under differential privacy (DP), where optimization is further complicated by noise injection and per-sample gradient clipping. While Maximal Update Parametrization ($μ$P) allows for zero-shot hyperparameter transfer in standard training, we show that it fails under DP constraints due to the distinct spectral properties of high-dimensional noise versus low-rank gradients. In this work, we introduce DP-$μ$P, a theoretically grounded framework that extends $μ$P to the privacy-preserving setting. By analyzing the interaction between gradient clipping, noise injection, and feature learning, we derive a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) condition that governs layer-wise learning rate scaling. Combining this with our proposed spectral scaling formulation, we provide specific scaling rules for DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon optimizers. Empirically, we demonstrate that DP-$μ$P enables effective zero-shot transfer of learning rates across model widths on diverse architectures (MLP, ViT, GPT-2), matching or exceeding the performance of individually tuned baselines while significantly reducing computational costs.

Machine Learning.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities
Machine Learning.summary: Understanding when neural networks learn interpretable representations is central to mechanistic interpretability. We study this through identifiability: when can supervised learning recover the true latent variables underlying the data? We introduce two data generating processes distinguished by their causal direction where either labels cause latents (generative) or latents cause labels (discriminative). When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space, we prove that the optimal encoders are linear in the latents. Conversely, when dimensions are insufficient, identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. We then show that additional constraints yield recovery of individual latent variables, not just linear mixtures. In the generative setting, non-negative activations and energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, providing a precise account of selective grandmother cell-like responses. In the discriminative setting, when latents are sparse and the true measurement matrix satisfies the spark condition, the learned encoder inherits compressed sensing structure, enabling sparse dictionary learning to perfectly recover individual latents. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis. Our framework unifies nonlinear ICA, compressed sensing, and neural network interpretability, delineating exactly when representations transition from nonlinear distortions to linear representations and, under additional constraints or steps, to clean, axis-aligned codes. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations drawn from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.

Machine Learning.title: DStill: Trajectory Consistency Distillation for Accelerated One-Step Drafting in Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
Machine Learning.summary: Block-diffusion speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting multiple tokens in parallel. However, one-step drafting in discrete diffusion is limited by token factorization error: each token is predicted from the same masked block, without conditioning on the tokens selected at other positions in that step. This can produce inconsistent drafts and reduce acceptance length. Iterative refinement mitigates this limitation by conditioning later predictions on previously committed tokens, though additional passes increase drafting cost. To address this trade-off between draft fidelity and inference latency, we introduce DStill, a two-stage framework that distills a target-conditioned drafter's own multi-step refinement into one-step drafting. We first train the drafter to complete partially revealed blocks, then use its refinement trajectories to train a student to predict the final completion in one pass. Using a curriculum that gradually transitions from partial to fully masked inputs, we successfully transfer the multi-step refinement capabilities into one step. Across reasoning, math, code benchmarks on three model families DStill improves acceptance length by up to 28% and speedup by up to 25% over one-step DFlash, achieving up to 6.45x speedup over auto-regressive decoding.

Machine Learning.title: LLM-Attack Suite: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
Machine Learning.summary: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attack Suite, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.

Machine Learning.title: Shaped SAEs: Expanding the Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability
Machine Learning.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) seek to decompose the dense activations of large language models (LLMs) into sparse, potentially interpretable features using a learned overcomplete dictionary. In this work, we ask whether it is possible to enhance the semantic selectivity of the learned dictionary atoms by linearly \emph{shaping} the dense activations prior to learning an SAE. We explore rank-reducing transformations based on the recently introduced J-space corresponding to the averaged Jacobian from the current layer to the LLM output, projecting activations onto the ``live'' subspace spanned by eigenmodes of the Jacobian with larger singular values (which we expect to be more semantically relevant). We also introduce a new approach for training SAEs in which (a)~an affine shaping transformation is learned along with the dictionary atoms, (b)~the atom selection mechanism is based on the TopK projections along the one-dimensional subspace spanned by the atoms, and (c)~reconstruction is carried out using the same atoms. We call this approach a Matched Filter SAE (MF-SAE) based on analogies with communication theory. The promise of shaping is demonstrated via evaluations against dense activations and state-of-the-art SAEs on benchmarks including SAEBench and SAE Probes.

Machine Learning.title: Knowledge That Is Linear Before Fine-Tuning Generalizes After It
Machine Learning.summary: Not all facts a language model can recall support further learning equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which can be recalled but do not support such generalization in a given task. We study this distinction by constructing new relations from existing ones. Take the relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris -> Europe) and assign each of its answers an arbitrary new label (Europe -> crab, Asia -> zebra). The new relation then maps Paris -> crab. We fine-tune the model on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the corresponding labels to held-out subjects that share an answer in the original relation. Having learned Paris -> crab, does it answer Munich -> crab? Across eleven language models and 70 relations, how linearly readable the original relation is in pretrained representations strongly predicts this generalization. Within each model, the two correlate across relations at Pearson r = 0.87 to 0.92. This association persists when controlling, separately and jointly, for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to re-randomizing the label assignment and fine-tuning seed, and to replacing the animal labels with labels from thirteen other semantic categories. When we map a fine-tuned model's wrong label back to the original answer it was assigned to, Munich -> zebra becomes Munich -> Asia. Answers recovered this way are more often among the linear probe's top answers for the subject than among the pretrained model's own. Whether a new relation generalizes depends less on whether its facts can be recalled than on how readily their shared structure can be read out linearly.
Machine Learning.comment: 25 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/NightMachinery/active-inert-facts

Machine Learning.title: Trail-Weighted Influence Scores for Approximate Outcome Prediction in Bayesian Networks
Machine Learning.summary: We study trail-weighted pruning of evidence for Bayesian-network prediction. A traversal enumerates the active trails from each evidence node to the outcome, scores each trail by the product of its edge strengths, and drops evidence whose score falls below a threshold. For collider-free networks (chains and forks) over binary variables, we show that the trail score equals the exact correlation between a trail's endpoints, that a chain and a fork with equal edge strengths have identical joint distributions, and that the pruned posterior is within a computable sum of per-trail terms of the exact posterior when each dropped trail lies in its own branch of the outcome node. We prove this bound, check it exhaustively on all small trees, and show that it fails when dropped trails share a branch. In simulations on random trees, thresholding trail scores gives 1.4 to 13 times lower error than random pruning of the same size. We also apply the score, as an unproven heuristic, to seven bnlearn networks with colliders and loops. Keeping the top half of the active evidence by trail score gives lower error than random pruning on all seven, but it is not clearly better than a mutual-information ranking, and scoring costs more than the inference it saves on six of the seven, so we show no speedup. Models trained on trail, graph and information features and tested on networks they never saw do not beat the trail score or mutual information, but trail features carry most of what they use and clearly outperform generic graph features. A bound for general networks is left to future work.
Machine Learning.comment: Research paper on approximate Bayesian-network inference, evidence pruning, theoretical error bounds, and empirical evaluation

Machine Learning.title: Predictive Closure: A Set-Level Characterization of JEPA's Feature Selection
Machine Learning.summary: In joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA), an encoder and a predictor are trained together to produce a representation that minimizes the error in predicting the representation of the next observation. Because the representations of both the current and the next observation are learned, it is unclear which features they will include. Earlier characterizations describe the features JEPA selects in terms of their individual predictability, raising the concern that unpredictable features, like a traffic light, will not be encoded into the representation. However, the prediction error is also affected by the relationships between features, e.g., the light's color helps predict whether the traffic will stop. We propose the predictive closure characterization, which accounts for these relationships. Based on a reformulation of the JEPA training objective, we show that selection depends on properties of feature sets. This view agrees with earlier works when features evolve independently, but makes new predictions when they do not, for instance that a feature like the traffic light can still be retained. We test this characterization in controlled experiments, which show that unpredictable features can become better represented when they help predict other features, and that changing one feature's predictive relationships can affect how well others are represented. We also demonstrate implications for steering feature selection: targeting one feature with an auxiliary objective, or supplying it to the predictor as side information, can strengthen the representation of another feature whose future values it helps predict, so steering can be indirect.

Machine Learning.title: HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient Mobile-Cloud Speculative Decoding
Machine Learning.summary: Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which runs the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head on the device to build a deep chain and uses one SLM pass to add alternative branches. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An ε-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three runs of each system on Spec-Bench show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-ε. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.
Machine Learning.comment: Under review at ACL Rolling Review (October 2026)
