To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.

Machine Learning.title: Decoupled Data Consistency with Diffusion Purification for Image Restoration
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion models have recently gained traction as a powerful class of deep generative priors, excelling in a wide range of image restoration tasks due to their exceptional ability to model data distributions. To solve image restoration problems, many existing techniques achieve data consistency by incorporating additional likelihood gradient steps into the reverse sampling process of diffusion models. However, the additional gradient steps pose a challenge for real-world practical applications as they incur a large computational overhead, thereby increasing inference time. They also present additional difficulties when using accelerated diffusion model samplers, as the number of data consistency steps is limited by the number of reverse sampling steps. In this work, we propose a novel diffusion-based image restoration solver that addresses these issues by decoupling the reverse process from the data consistency steps. Our method involves alternating between a reconstruction phase to maintain data consistency and a refinement phase that enforces the prior via diffusion purification. Our approach demonstrates versatility, making it highly adaptable for efficient problem-solving in latent space. Additionally, it reduces the necessity for numerous sampling steps through the integration of consistency models. The efficacy of our approach is validated through comprehensive experiments across various image restoration tasks, including image denoising, deblurring, inpainting, and super-resolution.

Machine Learning.title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
Machine Learning.summary: NVIDIA tensor cores have supported 2:4 semi-structured sparsity since Ampere, and the pattern composes with quantization. When the two are combined, the practical question is which step to take next: from a given precision, add 2:4 sparsity or drop to the next lower precision? We compare the two at equal bits, with sparsity metadata counted, and at equal nominal tensor-core tiers, over all six GEMM operands of a transformer layer, with kernels measured on three GPU generations and online pruning and quantization included. Our results show that as long as a lower precision is available, adding 2:4 is the worse step, both less accurate and slower, because the energy that 2:4 discards from each group of four along the hardware-forced axis does not shrink with bits, while quantization error does. Once quantization reaches the lowest precision the hardware supports, 2:4 still speeds up linear layers by 1.3--1.7\x{}, and on an H100 a retrained 2:4 model served in FP8 by vLLM reaches 27\% higher prefill throughput than the dense FP8 model, with GSM8K accuracy on par. Its quality has to be won back by retraining, however, which restores perplexity long before reasoning; on Blackwell, whose sparse FP4 uses a pairwise 4:8 pattern, the loss is larger and our retraining budget did not recover it.

Machine Learning.title: Zero-Shot Cross-City Generalization in End-to-End Autonomous Driving: Self-Supervised versus Supervised Representations
Machine Learning.summary: End-to-end autonomous driving models are typically trained on multi-city datasets using supervised ImageNet-pretrained backbones, yet their ability to generalize to unseen cities remains largely unexamined. When training and evaluation data are geographically mixed, models may implicitly rely on city-specific cues, masking failure modes that would occur under real-world domain shifts when generalizing to new locations. In this work, we formulate zero-shot cross-city transfer as a controlled representation-level stress test for end-to-end autonomous driving and ask how visual pretraining affects transfer behavior under geographic domain shift. We conduct a comprehensive study by integrating self-supervised backbones I-JEPA, DINOv2, and MAE into planning frameworks. We evaluate performance under strict geographic splits on nuScenes in the open-loop setting and on NAVSIM in the closed-loop evaluation protocol. Our experiments reveal a substantial generalization gap when transferring models across cities with different road topologies, traffic conventions, and visual environments. In open-loop evaluation, a supervised backbone exhibits severe degradation when transferring between cities, yet some domain-specific self-supervised methods can substantially reduce both displacement and collision degradation. In closed-loop evaluation, self-supervised pretraining improves average out-of-distribution PDMS in several single-city training settings. Our results provide empirical evidence that representation learning influences the robustness of cross-city planning and motivate zero-shot geographic transfer as an important stress test for evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving systems.

Machine Learning.title: NodeSynth: Socially Aligned Synthetic Data for AI Evaluation
Machine Learning.summary: Recent advancements in generative AI facilitate large-scale synthetic data generation for model evaluation. However, without targeted approaches, these datasets often lack the sociotechnical nuance required for sensitive domains. We introduce NodeSyn, a methodology that pairs a fine-tuned taxonomy generator (TaG) with credible published sources and extracted sensitive attributes to generate queries reflecting authentic societal contexts and nuanced harms. Evaluated across ten open-weight and proprietary LLMs in Medical Advice and Self-Harm using human-validated autoraters, NodeSyn ranked first on 8 of 10 models in each domain. NodeSyn datasets induced average failure rates 3.1 times higher than generic synthetic baselines, 2.4 times higher than structured synthetic benchmarks, and 1.6 times higher than authentic human-authored queries. Ablation studies confirm that, controlling for structural confounds, our granular Level 3 taxonomic expansion significantly drives these failure rates over Level 2 across 9 of 10 models (+29.2% relative lift in Medical Advice and +24.0% in Self-Harm). Variance attribution analysis reveals that failures are driven not only by what topics are queried (taxonomic nodes and lexical specificity), but also by their sociotechnical grounding (affected demographics, occupations, geographies, and querying personas). We embed this method into a research prototype, and open-source (https://github.com/google-research/nodesynth) the code and datasets to enable scalable, high-stakes model evaluation

Machine Learning.title: Multi-Objective Protein Optimization via Modular Diffusion Steering
Machine Learning.summary: Protein engineering often requires improving several properties simultaneously, motivating the search for high-performing sequences that represent useful fitness tradeoffs. Discovering these sequences is challenging because the design space is combinatorially large and experimental campaigns often permit only a few rounds of batched measurements. We introduce \textit{MODS}, a modular framework for multi-objective protein optimization via inference-time diffusion steering. For each proposal, MODS samples augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and a fitness-surrogate ensemble member to define a scalar steering reward. Varying the weights directs generation toward different objective tradeoffs, while varying ensemble members diversifies the predictions used for guidance. Because MODS expresses multi-objective acquisition through scalar rewards, it can be paired with different diffusion models and compatible steering procedures. After each evaluation batch, MODS updates the surrogates without retraining the generative model. We evaluate MODS on six protein optimization tasks using predictive oracles trained on experimental assay data, with two diffusion models and two steering procedures. MODS achieves competitive final hypervolume across all six tasks with both diffusion models, and substantially outperforms the best evaluated baseline on several tasks. Our results demonstrate a flexible and effective approach to multi-objective protein optimization with limited feedback.

Machine Learning.title: Auditing Conformal Prediction for Language Models Under Inference-Time Model Shift
Machine Learning.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is typically evaluated under a matched protocol, in which calibration and deployment use the same post-training inference configuration, such as quantization mode and inference temperature. In deployment, these choices often differ from those used at calibration to meet memory or throughput constraints or serving policies. We argue that this exposes a limitation in current CP evaluation protocols for language models. We formalize the underlying phenomenon as inference-time model shift: a change in the conformal score distribution induced by inference configuration rather than by the input--label distribution, and theoretically characterize how it breaks split-conformal exchangeability even when the task distribution and trained model are unchanged. We then evaluate its consequences across 8 language models, 4 finite-label benchmarks, and 12 inference configurations. We find that matched evaluation can substantially overstate deployment-time coverage, and that the effect is heterogeneous across models and datasets. We argue that inference configuration should be reported as a first-class experimental axis in CP evaluations for language-model systems.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets

Machine Learning.title: When Retain Constraints Conflict: Mitigating Forget-Retain Interference in Tabular Data
Machine Learning.summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data while preserving model utility, but its behavior on tabular data remains underexplored. This gap is important because tabular prediction is widely used in high-stakes domains and is increasingly adapted to language models through record serialization and schema-aware prompting. We identify a key challenge that distinguishes tabular unlearning from unlearning in free-form text or other modalities: schema-induced forget-retain overlap. In serialized tabular data, records share fixed column-name/value slots, similar attribute ranges, and common output spaces. Consequently, a forget row may have nearby retain rows that rely on the same high-signal attributes, causing retain preservation to oppose the update required for forgetting. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose Conflict-Aware Unlearning (CAU), a schema-aware approach that reduces forget-retain interference by relaxing preservation constraints on retained rows that most conflict with the forget set. Across sample-level and feature-level unlearning on clinical and non-medical tabular tasks, CAU more closely matches a retraining oracle while maintaining predictive utility and retain-region behavior. Our results show that reliable tabular LLM unlearning depends not only on the forgetting objective, but also on how retain constraints are constructed.

Machine Learning.title: DrugReason: Dynamic Multi-View Reasoning over Knowledge Graph and Language Evidence for Drug Repurposing
Machine Learning.summary: Drug repurposing aims to identify new therapeutic uses for existing compounds and, compared with de novo drug discovery, offers a faster and more cost-effective path to clinical translation. However, the space of candidate drug-disease pairs is enormous and their underlying relationships often depend on complex multi-hop biological mechanisms, making it difficult to reliably predict which pairs represent true therapeutic relationships. Existing approaches tackle this from two directions: knowledge graph-based methods organize curated biomedical evidence into structured relational networks for grounded multi-hop reasoning, while LLM-based methods leverage pretrained knowledge to generate flexible mechanistic rationales. Yet neither is sufficient alone - KGs are confined to observed graph structure while LLMs lack factual grounding and risk hallucination. To address this gap, we propose DrugReason, a multi-view reasoning framework that integrates grounded KG reasoning with LLM-generated mechanistic inference for drug repurposing. DrugReason adaptively routes diverse reasoning paths to specialized experts conditioned on the query context, while a cross-expert distillation objective enables knowledge sharing without sacrificing expert specialization. Experiments on PharmaDB, DDInter, and DrugBank show that DrugReason improves average performance over strong single-view reasoning baselines and achieves competitive or superior results compared with graph-based alternatives, while providing interpretable routing-based predictions.

Machine Learning.title: The Data Differentiator Framework (DDF): Quantifying Marginal Data Value with Information-Theoretic and Game-Theoretic Measures in an Agentic Evaluation Pipeline (SDSAE)
Machine Learning.summary: In data-rich enterprises the hard question is not whether a candidate dataset is good in isolation, but whether it adds information beyond what the organization already holds, and whether that increment is worth its price. We present the Data Differentiator Framework (DDF), a composite scoring method for candidate data assets that combines (i) a mutual-information-based redundancy penalty against the existing portfolio, (ii) a cost-normalized, significance-gated marginal utility score derived from an ablation study, and (iii) explicit governance inputs (trust, identity resolution quality, strategic weights) set by the business. The framework is executed by a staged pipeline, the Strategic Data Sourcing Agent Ecosystem (SDSAE), that short-circuits expensive model-retraining steps for assets failing governance or redundancy gates. Conceptually, the DDF extends the relevance-minus-redundancy principle of mRMR feature selection from the feature level to the asset level, and adds cost normalization, a statistical significance gate, and governance terms that per-sample valuation methods such as Data Shapley do not model. We validate the framework on the public credit-card fraud benchmark (284,807 transactions) with five constructed candidate assets spanning the redundancy spectrum. Only the genuinely differentiated asset passes the significance gate ($Δ$AUC = +0.0029, DeLong $p = 1.4\times 10^{-9}$, Holm-corrected $p = 7.2\times 10^{-9}$) and receives an acquire recommendation (DDS = +0.663); the fully redundant asset scores lowest (DDS = -0.135). The recommendation is stable across 19 of 22 admissible strategic-weight configurations and across all decision thresholds in [0.15, 0.66]. We state clearly which quantities in the case study are computed from data and which are simulated governance inputs, and we discuss the design limits of a single-dataset evaluation.
Machine Learning.comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Primary cs.AI; cross-listed cs.LG and stat.ML

Machine Learning.title: Adaptive Pluralistic Alignment: A pipeline for dynamic artificial democracy
Machine Learning.summary: Prevailing alignment methods target a fixed set of preferences and therefore risk forcing value lock-in as societal norms evolve over time. We introduce Adaptive Pluralistic Alignment (APA), a modular pipeline for updating pluralistically aligned AI systems to track evolving values and avoid value lock-in without repeating costly pretraining or large-scale data collection. APA has three stages: (1) learning compact personalized reward models via low-rank reward basis decomposition, (2) using these models as a jury that collectively selects among candidate outputs through social-choice-theoretic voting, and (3) efficiently adapting the jury over time by fitting new annotator weights over the fixed reward bases as values shift. The resulting system is efficient, explainable, steerable, and modular. We implement a proof-of-concept instantiation using simulated historical annotators, demonstrate how jury composition and the choice of voting rule can substantially affect outcomes, and bound value tracking error given a sliding-window jury. We provide full code at https://github.com/RachelFreedman/apa.

Machine Learning.title: SAGE: Semantic Audio Generative Encoder
Machine Learning.summary: Audio autoencoders compress waveforms into compact latent representations that serve as the interface between raw audio and downstream models. Current systems navigate a three-way trade-off between reconstruction quality, semantic structure of the latent space, and inference speed, typically favoring one or two of these at the expense of the others. This paper introduces SAGE, Semantic Audio Generative Encoder: a compact variational autoencoder, trained solely on publicly available music, that shapes its latent by distilling embeddings from a pretrained audio-text model. This 105M-parameter model runs about 3x faster than Stable Audio Open and reaches the listening-test quality of SAME-L, an autoencoder 8x larger and over 2x slower, while surpassing both on objective perceptual and distributional metrics of reconstruction. Furthermore, it sets the state of the art on all nineteen probing tasks of latent semantics, in domain and out of domain. These results establish SAGE as a lightweight audio autoencoder that strikes the best balance of the three-way trade-off among those we evaluate, combining high reconstruction fidelity, state-of-the-art semantic structure, and fast inference.
Machine Learning.comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Code and weights: https://github.com/francescobrigante/SAGE. Project page: https://sage-music.pages.dev/ v3: inference times re-measured on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU in TF32, with a revised protocol and all numerical precisions in Appendix C; speed claims updated accordingly. Training, reconstruction, listening-test and probing results are unchanged

Machine Learning.title: One Policy, Many Styles: Where to Aggregate Preferences for Steerable Humanoid Control?
Machine Learning.summary: Modern robotic agents are increasingly expected to support steerable control, where a single policy can adjust its behavioral style at runtime under changing user preferences. Preference-conditioned reinforcement learning provides this interface, but conditioning alone does not ensure that a requested behavior change is strong, does not leak into unrelated behaviors, and does not compromise task performance. Our evaluation combines Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR) with coverage and utility metrics. We use these measures to compare reward-level, advantage-level, loss-level, and PCGrad-based aggregation across two humanoid-control frameworks. No aggregation level performs best across all environments and criteria. Experiments show that aggregating objectives early produces a wider range of behavioral responses but greater unintended changes in other objectives, while aggregating them later improves control precision at some cost to responsiveness.

Machine Learning.title: Query Feedback and Teaching for Stable and Certifiable Language Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Language generation in the limit studies whether a learner observing an enumeration of an unknown target language can eventually generate only valid, previously unseen elements. We study stability, introduced by Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Velegkas (2025), which requires the generator's infinite output set to eventually remain unchanged, and introduce the stronger notion of certifiability, which requires the generator to determine from its observations that its current output is valid. Drawing on teaching sets in learning theory, we introduce a hierarchy of teaching dimensions for generation under three increasingly strict success criteria: correctness, stability, and certifiability. These dimensions measure the minimum number of selected examples whose appearance guarantees the corresponding success condition. We also study stability and certifiability in the membership-query model of Charikar and Pabbaraju (2025). We characterize stable and certifiable generation, both with and without query feedback, and establish their relationships with uniform generation and identification in the limit. In particular, we give a finite-witness characterization of stable generation, analogous to Angluin's tell-tale characterization of identification, resolving a gap left open by Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Velegkas (2025). We further compare these generation notions with identification in the limit and contrast their teaching requirements on well-studied language families, including regular and erasing pattern languages.

Machine Learning.title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees
Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.

Machine Learning.title: Telling FIBS: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception
Machine Learning.summary: Recent incidents have highlighted the challenge of monitoring LLM agents and the danger of models deceiving people. We show that white-box deception detection via probes can be scaled up to frontier monitoring settings by collecting the largest deception dataset to date for training probes and introducing a novel probe architecture which can aggregate information across many layers and tokens. Our probes surpass black-box monitors on agentic coding benchmarks, achieving 98.3% AUROC in SHADE-Arena and 98.0% in BashArena (vs. 97.7%, 97.6% resp. for action-only text monitors), and show improved efficacy as the underlying model is scaled up. We further test probes on several cases where deception cannot be determined from the context alone; in these cases of introspective deception, the ground truth can only be determined through careful elicitation or knowledge of a model's training data. In one such evaluation, we show that probes can distinguish transcripts containing a model's true hidden goal from other goals with an AUROC of up to 99.7%. Our probes also detect deception on prominent open-weight models which lie about politically sensitive topics when put under pressure. We release our training dataset, dubbed FIBS, to help drive frontier deployment of effective probes, and encourage the community to expand upon it with further examples of deception and sabotage.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages main text, 119 pages total; 26 figures, 28 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/fibs-probes

Machine Learning.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
Machine Learning.summary: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.

Machine Learning.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
Machine Learning.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

Machine Learning.title: Fine-Tuning Small Reasoning Models for Quantum Field Theory
Machine Learning.summary: Despite the growing application of large language models (LLMs) to theoretical physics, there has been little academic exploration of how domain-specific physics reasoning ability develops during training. To investigate this, we perform the first academic comparison of reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning for LLMs on verifiable problem-solving tasks in theoretical physics. Because the open-source verifiable training data required to develop such capabilities is scarce, we built a robust data generation pipeline that can both create synthetic problems and make existing human-authored problems suitable for model training. Selecting quantum field theory (QFT) as our primary domain, we generated over 2,500 synthetic problems alongside a curated collection of human-adapted problems sourced from arXiv and standard pedagogical resources. We conduct both reinforcement learning (RL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) experiments, benchmarking performance gains as well as generalization to other physics domains. Although both methods improve over the base model on every dataset, SFT gains are concentrated on in-distribution synthetic tasks, while RL generalizes better, outperforming SFT on the human-adapted datasets and TPBench. We perform an extensive analysis of model chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before and after fine-tuning to understand how reasoning errors evolve during RL and SFT. Finally, we publicly release our data pipeline, verifiable QFT training data, and ~200M tokens of QFT reasoning traces.
Machine Learning.comment: Updating arXiv after publication in IOP Science MLST Journal with minor revisions to the original pre-print

Machine Learning.title: Tropical Cyclone Attributes in Sparse Autoencoder Features of an AI Weather Model
Machine Learning.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) weather models now forecast weather events skillfully, but how they represent these events internally remains unknown. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide sparse features for probing hidden states, but how information about multiple physical attributes of an event is organized across them remains unclear. Using tropical cyclones in GraphCast as a test case, we analyze 2,115 six-hourly timesteps from 205 cyclones, relating SAE activations to position, intensity, and pressure structure across five Layer-8 decompositions and 16 processor layers. Each attribute relates to multiple features; position and pressure-structure relations overlap in a smaller subset. This organization recurs across independent SAEs and layers without feature alignment. In deeper layers, the leading position feature aligns better with position and pressure structure six hours ahead than at present. These results suggest that the organization of physical-attribute relations provides a reproducible level of description for interpreting cyclone-related information in GraphCast.
Machine Learning.comment: 22 pages, 4 figures; supporting information included as an ancillary file. Submitted to Geophysical Research Letters

Machine Learning.title: MCLR: Improving Conditional Modeling via Inter-Class Likelihood-Ratio Maximization and Unifying Classifier-Free Guidance with Alignment Objectives
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion models achieve strong generative performance but often rely on classifier-free guidance (CFG), an inference-time intervention that modifies the sampling trajectory. Since standard denoising score matching (DSM) should recover the target distribution when the score is learned accurately, the practical necessity of CFG suggests deficiencies in learned conditional scores. We identify weak inter-class separation as one such limitation: samples generated from the same noise under different labels can retain similar class-agnostic structure. To address this deficiency, we introduce MCLR, a principled fine-tuning objective that explicitly maximizes inter-class likelihood-ratios, thereby strengthening class-specific structures under standard sampling. Across diverse models and datasets, MCLR substantially improves guidance-free conditional generation and narrows the gap to CFG. Theoretically, we prove that the CFG-guided score is the unique minimizer of a sample-adaptively weighted, ELBO-approximated MCLR objective, interpreting CFG as an implicit inference-time contrastive alignment procedure. We further compare MCLR with related contrastive objectives, including DPO, CCA, and CFM, clarifying their connections and key differences in an otherwise fragmented literature.

Machine Learning.title: Minimax-Optimal Predictive Flow Matching under Distribution Drift
Machine Learning.summary: Flow matching learns a generative velocity field by regression, but under distribution drift a field must be deployed before the current data arrive. We study this predictive problem for a fixed, possibly nonconvex, neural class, with dynamic regret against the best represented field of each round. We propose DyProd-FM, which refits flow matching on dyadic historical prefixes and selects among the fits with a sleeping Prod master. Without knowing any drift budget, it attains regret $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_ω+1,1+\sqrt{TΩ}\})$ in the relative velocity risk variation $Ω$ and $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_μ+1,1+T^{1/3}V_μ^{2/3}\})$ in the target-law variation $V_μ=\sum_t W_2(μ_{t+1},μ_t)$, up to approximation and fitting costs. Matching lower bounds for fixed classes show that both rates are optimal in $T$ and in the budgets up to logarithmic factors. Prior optimal dynamic-regret guarantees rely on a convex decision set with strongly convex or exp-concave losses, whereas our class may be nonconvex and no curvature in its parameters is assumed. The target-law rate rests on a second-order link between the two variations, which the base noise of flow matching provides.

Machine Learning.title: Is Refusal Direction Universal across Low-Resourced Languages?
Machine Learning.summary: Refusal directions have been shown to transfer cross-lingually with near-perfect effectiveness across safety-aligned languages (Wang et al., 2025), reportedly regardless of resource level. However, the only truly low-resourced language evaluated is Yoruba, which is strongly misaligned and shows limited transfer, leaving open how refusal directions behave for other low-resourced languages. We extend PolyRefuse to three additional low-resourced languages (Belarusian, Bashkir, and Tajik) and replicate the pipeline of (Wang et al., 2025) on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. We find that universality is graded rather than binary: directions from safety-aligned and partially-aligned languages transfer broadly, while those from strongly misaligned languages fail to reliably modulate refusal behavior on any target tested, including other misaligned languages, once ceiling effects are accounted for. Geometric alignment and behavioral transfer are further shown to be partially dissociated. These findings complicate the universality claim and suggest that users of the least-resourced, most strongly misaligned languages may face weaker safety guarantees.

Machine Learning.title: CSD: Common-Support Distillation for Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Transfer
Machine Learning.summary: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation enables knowledge transfer across model families, allowing students to learn from stronger or more specialized teachers. However, differences in vocabulary and segmentation make teacher and student next-token distributions difficult to align. Existing logits-based methods are easy to integrate into standard distillation pipelines, but often rely on restrictive heuristics or tokenizer-pair-specific choices. They may restrict supervision to shared vocabulary subsets, require manually selecting different objectives for different tokenizer pairs, or match only the observed chunk and its complement rather than individual alternative continuations. We introduce Common-Support Distillation (CSD), a unified logits-based framework that constructs a shared support between the teacher and student at each aligned input chunk and matches the induced distributions with a single objective. For one-to-one alignments, CSD uses explicit common-token pairs as the shared support. For other alignments, it constructs a virtual support whose probabilities are computed using the autoregressive chain rule. A residual event captures probability mass outside the explicit support, ensuring that both induced distributions remain normalized. Across four teacher-student settings comprising Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B-PT students with Qwen and Phi teachers, CSD consistently achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated cross-tokenizer methods, outperforming the strongest alternative by up to 1.8 points and surpassing both continued pretraining and same-tokenizer distillation. For Llama-3.1-8B, CSD improves average accuracy over the strongest evaluated baseline by up to 4.2 points for the base student and 1.6 points for the instruction-tuned student.

Machine Learning.title: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Domain Adaptation via Knowledge Recasting
Machine Learning.summary: Adapting language models to new domains during post-training risks degrading previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon commonly known as catastrophic forgetting. Existing mitigation methods largely treat forgetting as a consequence of excessive model drift. They therefore constrain updates by preserving old outputs, replaying old data, or regularizing changes to parameters and representations so that the updated model remains close to its previous state. We take a different view: Rather than pulling the updated model back toward its old state, we translate the new domain into the model's pre-existing knowledge space, making unfamiliar knowledge learnable through familiar procedures. Therefore, we propose Skill Schema Transport (SST), a post-training framework that transports new knowledge into the model's existing skill space. SST abstracts each example type into a skill schema, preserving its essential operations, dependencies, and verification steps while removing domain-specific surface forms. By recasting new examples as instances of reusable procedures, SST turns knowledge update from trajectory memorization into procedural reuse. In continual domain adaptation settings, SST consistently reduces forgetting while improving generalization to related tasks. Across two 3B instruction-tuned backbones, SST improves average final performance on streamed domains by 2.53 to 5.75 points over sequential post-training. It also lowers max-drop forgetting in all evaluated settings, with the largest reduction from 42.41 to 7.10 points on the Qwen-3B MATH stream, while substantially recovering the OOD degradation induced by sequential updates.

Machine Learning.title: TrustAgent-RFF: Agentic Diagnostic Planning for Reliable RF Fingerprinting under Domain Shift
Machine Learning.summary: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.
Machine Learning.comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to INFOCOM

Machine Learning.title: CellTwin: Reproducible Cellular Network Emulation via High Resolution, in situ Measurement-Driven ML
Machine Learning.summary: Current and future applications demand ultra-low latency and consistent throughput, yet frequently traverse 5G cellular networks, so cope with volatile packet dynamics, as 5G base station schedulers dynamically react to user workloads and wireless channel conditions. The task of evaluating network algorithms in these environments is hamstrung by current tools: record-and-replay emulators sever the feedback interaction that exists between application end points and a commercial operator's proprietary 5G scheduler, while full-stack simulators rely on overly simplistic scheduling logic. To bridge this reality gap, we present NeuralEmu, a high-fidelity, machine learning-based emulation framework that learns complex 5G scheduler resource allocation behaviors directly from extremely high-resolution network telemetry tools. The first emulator to handle multiple clients, NeuralEmu utilizes machine learning to dynamically predict resource block allocations and modulation schemes based on instantaneous user buffer occupancy and channel states. To capture realistic cross-user contention, a traffic reconstruction model inverts cellular network scheduling results to recover the underlying traffic patterns of uncontrolled background users. Implemented as an high-performance Linux middlebox emulator, NeuralEmu reduces emulation error relative to the state of the art for various network applications including but not limited to 55% for web-page load time, 57% for WebRTC encoder bit rate, and 51% for cloud gaming packet one-way delay, providing an accurate, standardized testing ground for tomorrow's real-time interactive network protocols and applications.

Machine Learning.title: Inverse RL Helps Align AI by Imitating Humans
Machine Learning.summary: Language model alignment aims to make model behavior reflect desirable properties such as helpfulness, safety, and instruction following. Existing methods draw supervision from expert demonstrations, preference judgments, or verifiable outcomes. Demonstrations typically guide supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while preference judgments and verifiers provide rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). This raises a question: can the demonstrations alone be used to derive an explicit, interpretable reward useful in a post-training pipeline? Motivated by inverse reinforcement learning, we introduce Projected Alignment Reward Estimated from Demonstrations (PARED). PARED learns an explicit reward from expert demonstrations over a small set of response-level features, using a lightweight discriminator that separates demonstrations from the policy's own samples in this feature space. Experiments with inference-time reranking and adversarial on-policy RL show improvements both when starting from a base model without an SFT stage and when further optimizing an SFT-trained model. Additionally, we demonstrate that PARED can be used for contextual alignment, in which a single policy learns to adapt its responses to the preferences of different audiences.

Machine Learning.title: RL-IF: Tracking Non-local Training Data Influence for Online Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success in decision-making tasks, but modern online RL remains highly sensitive to the quality of training experience. Understanding the contribution of individual training instances is therefore central to data-centric RL, with applications ranging from experience selection to policy interpretation. Existing data attribution methods for online RL primarily focus on local influence within a single training round, overlooking the non-local data influence across multiple training rounds. In this work, we formalize data attribution in online RL through a trajectory-level leave-one-out quantity, RL-LOO, which measures how one training sample influences a downstream target after subsequent online updates have taken place. We then derive RL-IF, a first-order estimator that propagates data influence through both optimization effects and policy-induced sampling effects, and provide theoretical guarantees on its approximation accuracy under smoothness assumptions. Our analysis further disentangles these two effects and shows both theoretically and empirically that the full RL-IF estimator can often be well approximated using the optimization effect alone. Building on this observation, we develop RINSE, a practical data filtering method for online RL. Experiments on standard control benchmarks and an RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation setting show that RINSE improves training efficiency and final performance over standard PPO and local attribution baselines. These results suggest that RL-IF provides a practical and principled framework for understanding and improving online RL.

Machine Learning.title: MARS: Harmonizing Multimodal Convergence via Adaptive Rank Search
Machine Learning.summary: Fine-tuning Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with parameter-efficient methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is crucial for task adaptation. However, imbalanced training dynamics across modalities often lead to suboptimal accuracy due to negative interference, a challenge typically addressed with inefficient heuristic methods such as manually tuning separate learning rates. To overcome this, we introduce MARS (Multimodal Adaptive Rank Search), an approach to discover optimal rank pairs that balance training dynamics while maximizing performance. Our key innovation, a proposed framework of dual scaling laws, enables this search: one law models module-specific convergence time to prune the search space to candidates with aligned dynamics, while the other predicts final task performance to select the optimal pair from the pruned set. By re-purposing the LoRA rank as a controller for modality-specific convergence speed, MARS outperforms baseline methods and provides a robust, automated strategy for optimizing MLLM fine-tuning.
Machine Learning.comment: NeurIPS 2026; Project Page: this https URL: https://minkyoungcho.github.io/mars/

Machine Learning.title: Actually, All Learnable Distribution Classes Are Privately Learnable
Machine Learning.summary: We show that every class of distributions that is learnable up to arbitrarily small target error in total variation distance with finitely many samples is also learnable under ($\varepsilon, δ$)-differential privacy up to arbitrarily small target error with finitely many samples. This proves a conjecture of Ashtiani. Previous work by Bun, Kamath, Mouzakis, and Singhal [arXiv:2402.00267] gave a weak refutation of this conjecture, showing that this implication is not true when learnability is defined with respect to a fixed target error. In contrast, we show that, under the standard definition of learnability, the conjecture is true.

Machine Learning.title: LEAN: Loss-Engineered Modulation of the Model Weight-Sensitivity Distribution for Efficient, Error-Tolerant Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: The weights of a trained network do not have uniform sensitivity to model accuracy: the 1% most sensitive weights carry about a fifth of the damage a bit flip can do. This distribution decides the bit-flip tolerance of a model, the fraction of weights a code must cover and the bits each weight needs; existing schemes work with the distribution training leaves. We show that we can systematically modulate or alter the weight sensitivity distribution of a trained model, thereby shifting weights from one sensitivity bin to another. The sensitivity of a stored weight is the product of its gradient and the step a flip takes in the storage format, and LEAN adds a composite regularizer on both factors, a range term that bounds the flip step and a tail term that lowers the gradient of the most sensitive weights, with one coefficient λ setting how far the distribution moves. Ten epochs with the term, as a fine-tune or as the last epochs of training, shrink the sensitive tail 5 to 13 times on nine vision models (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet) within 0.5 points of accuracy; real flips confirm that the reshaped weights do less damage, a plain gradient-norm penalty does not reproduce the effect, and a preliminary extension to three small language models shows the same tail shaping. With a BCH code over 1% of the weights the model then survives 300 progressive bit-search flips in every training seed and 500 in two of three, where three of four published defenses with the same code fail by 300 and WCAT falls to 75% at 500. The reshaped distribution also cuts the parity for a fixed guarantee 3.7 times and makes a sensitivity-ordered 8/6/4/3-bit format affordable, which stores ImageNet ResNet-50 at a 3.29-bit weight payload, 2.4 times smaller than INT8, above the accuracy of LSQ at 3 bits.

Machine Learning.title: How Much Gradient Does Truncated Backprop Lose in Looped Transformers?
Machine Learning.summary: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops. We measure how much of the weight gradient this throws away, exactly and for every k from one backward pass, on nine looped language models, and report three findings. First, on a trained model this lost gradient is set near the output: once the loop count is well above k, it barely changes with the loop count (within about 0.03 from 32 to 64 loops on the three models we tested, as a pre-registered test predicted for Parcae). Where the backward signal shrinks, $ρ^k$, with $ρ$ the signal's fitted shrink per loop, approximates it at moderate loop counts but overstates it at long ones, because the fitted $ρ$ drifts up as the fit takes in more loops. On Ouro the signal grows, and keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient. Second, the lost gradient falls during fine-tuning, by 0.07-0.22 within 300 steps on three of four models, on held-out problems too. The fall is not just the read-out's share of the gradient; training only the layers outside the loop reproduced up to half of it, and it also falls under truncated training. So a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. Third, we could not show that it predicts the training cost of truncation better than rules that need no measurement: on two new models it tied Parcae's cost at the same k, in a test too small to separate them.
Machine Learning.comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Code, pre-registrations and results: https://github.com/Aur-Shalev-Merin/lost-gradient-looped-transformers

Machine Learning.title: Interpretable but Fragile? Robustness of Concept Bottlenecks under Geometric-Semantic Perturbations
Machine Learning.summary: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) are designed to provide interpretable intermediate representations, yet how such bottlenecks affect robustness remains unclear, with existing studies reporting mixed and sometimes contradictory findings. We argue that these discrepancies arise from conflating different robustness notions and perturbation regimes, rather than from fundamental disagreements about CBMs themselves. To disentangle these factors, we introduce a generator-based evaluation framework that enables controlled comparisons between standard classifiers and CBMs under two distinct perturbation types: continuous geometric perturbations in latent space and discrete semantic interventions in concept space. Within this framework, we evaluate robustness both empirically, via prediction and concept-level sensitivity metrics, and certifiably, using randomized smoothing in latent and concept spaces. Across experiments, we reconcile previously conflicting findings by clarifying when, and in what sense, concept bottlenecks do or do not improve robustness. By further analyzing robustness under varying task conditions, including class semantic similarity and concept vocabulary size, we show that interpretability does not inherently confer robustness. Instead, concept bottlenecks shift where and how sensitivity manifests, revealing a nuanced interpretability robustness trade off that depends critically on the perturbation regime and task structure. Together, our results show that interpretability and robustness are distinct objectives: interpretable intermediate representations do not uniformly improve robustness, but instead redistribute sensitivity across perturbation spaces and model families.

Machine Learning.title: A General Topological Symmetry Index for Critical Orbits In Neural Network Loss Landscapes
Machine Learning.summary: A systematic understanding of the global structure of neural-network loss landscapes remains challenging due to their high dimensionality. Symmetries arising from network architectures and learning objectives provide a way to investigate aspects of this structure. Although a growing number of studies have drawn attention to these symmetries, a systematic characterization of them, as well as of the critical orbits they give rise to, remains incomplete. To address this gap, in this work we establish a topological symmetry index, based on the methodologies from the family of equivariant degree theories, to decode these symmetries. The frameworks apply to arbitrary network architectures and include methods applicable to degenerate critical orbits. The index detects the isotropy of the critical points and quantifies the corresponding net topological contributions. Several examples, including softplus MLPs, Transformers, and equivariant neural networks, are presented to illustrate the computations.

Machine Learning.title: DualHeads: Reward-tilted few-step diffusion made simple
Machine Learning.summary: Distilled diffusion models generate high-quality images in a few sampling steps, but aligning them with task requirements and human preferences is difficult. Methods developed for multi-step diffusion models rely on differentiable rewards, or on score fields and stochastic trajectories that distilled generators may lack. We ask whether a few-step generator can be adapted using only external reward evaluations and reference samples, and show that two binary classifiers suffice. Our method, DualHeads, implements them as lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. The reward head learns which samples of the same prompt score higher, the reference head separates reference images from generated ones, and the generator maximizes a weighted sum of their logits. When the heads are optimal, this objective is KL-regularized maximization of the learned reward, and the ratio of head weights sets the regularization strength. Empirically, with both rule-based and model-based rewards, a few-step DualHeads generator reaches task rewards close to those of 40-step reinforcement learning methods while preserving image quality, at no extra inference cost. We hope that this simple and elegant dual-head formulation will help advance few-step reward-tilted generation.

Machine Learning.title: Spatiotemporal Reconstruction of Global Radiation from Sparse Sensor Sequences
Machine Learning.summary: Much of the physical world is inaccessible to direct measurement and can be reached only through the sparse traces it leaves in other observable variables. Here we introduce the Temporal Radiation Operator Network (TRON), a spatiotemporal neural operator that learns proxy-to-field mappings, reconstructing otherwise unobserved physical fields from sparse, indirect sensor histories. For cosmic-radiation mapping, TRON reconstructs sea-level effective dose at 65,341 locations from histories of 12 neutron monitors, achieving 0.096\% mean relative $L_2$ error against EXPACS-generated reference fields in a chronologically held-out year; batched GPU inference evaluates a global field in approximately $\sim$1~ms, compared with $\sim$57.6~s for EXPACS on one CPU thread. On measured weather networks, TRON reconstructs temperature at held-out stations from thermometer or barometer histories, outperforming interpolation, calendar-based and hypsometric baselines. These results establish proxy-to-field reconstruction as a general route to recovering spatially distributed physical information beyond the direct reach of sparse sensor networks.

Machine Learning.title: From Fuzzy to Exact: The Halo Architecture for Infinite-Depth Reasoning via Rational Arithmetic
Machine Learning.summary:
The prevailing scaling paradigm of Large Language Models (LLMs) rests on a substrate of "Fuzzy" floating-point arithmetic. To mitigate the inherent instability of this approximate foundation, modern architectures have erected a complex scaffolding of structural and numerical heuristics--Complex Residuals, Pre-RMSNorm, Attention Scaling, and Gradient Clipping--consuming significant compute solely to prevent numerical collapse.
  We propose a paradigm shift to the "Exact". We introduce the Halo Architecture, grounded in the Rational Field (Q) and powered by a custom Exact Inference Unit (EIU). To resolve the exponential bit-width growth of rational arithmetic, Halo employs a Dual-Ring Topology that unifies two complementary control mechanisms: (1) The Micro-Ring (Continuum Maintenance), which strictly bounds memory complexity via Diophantine Approximation; and (2) The Macro-Ring (Symbolic Alignment), which enforces logical consistency via periodic state collapse.
  This stable dual-ring substrate allows for the "Great Dismantling" of numerical scaffolding, reducing the Transformer block to its "Clean" algebraic form (Tabula Rasa). Furthermore, we verify the "Efficiency Paradox": the elimination of gradient noise (sigma -> 0) allows for Macro-Learning Rates, potentially reducing the Total Time-to-Convergence by orders of magnitude. Halo demonstrates that General Intelligence requires the hybridization of continuous fields and discrete chains under a rigorous mathematical framework.
Machine Learning.comment: Revised in response to feedback received during the Conference on Next Generation Arithmetic (CoNGA) review process. Added formal analysis of precision-escalation termination and Diophantine approximation error bounds; expanded related work

Machine Learning.title: Self-Supervised Tuning of Low-Fidelity Optimization Models via High-Fidelity Feedback
Machine Learning.summary: Low-fidelity (LF) optimization models are widely used in large-scale operations because they can be solved efficiently and reliably, but they often exhibit systematic errors relative to high-fidelity (HF) formulations that better capture physical and operational constraints. Existing learning-based approaches typically rely on supervised or semi-supervised training with HF solutions, which are expensive to compute and may not align with HF operational objectives. We propose a self-supervised framework that parameterizes LF optimization models directly from HF feedback. The low-fidelity problem is embedded as a differentiable optimization layer and trained end-to-end, while a HF correction problem evaluates its solution and provides gradient information through its dual variables, without requiring HF solution labels. We evaluate the framework on optimal power flow, optimal gas flow, and pooling problems, spanning different sources of low- and high-fidelity mismatch. Across all three applications, the self-supervised approach improves objective quality and feasibility over untuned LF models and generally outperforms semi-supervised training. The learned parameterizations also generalize to unseen operating conditions and, for network applications with up to 30,000 nodes, to systems not encountered during training.

Machine Learning.title: SeFoRA: Sketch-Aggregated Federated Low-Rank Adaptation with Heterogeneous Client Ranks
Machine Learning.summary: We consider federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning of foundation models, e.g., LLMs and LVMs, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA; ~Hu et al.\ 2022). Combining LoRA with federated learning introduces challenges absent from either setting alone: clients may use different LoRA ranks, making their factor matrices dimension-incompatible, and factor-wise averaging suffers from a bilinear mismatch. We propose SeFoRA, a sketch-aggregated federated LoRA algorithm in which each client transmits a linear sketch of its local $Δ\mathbf{W}$ updates, enabling direct aggregation at the federator. As a result, SeFoRA overcomes the rank heterogeneity challenge and alleviates the bilinear mismatch. We establish convergence to a neighborhood of a first-order stationary point at rate $\\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$. Extensive numerical experiments on language and vision models showcase the performance of our algorithm compared to existing methods.

Machine Learning.title: When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning
Machine Learning.summary:
Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space. For base generation this default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, however, it carries a structural limitation. The standard VAE's KL term does not merely ignore mode structure - it actively taxes separation and tightness. When data are multimodal, the ELBO optimum compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, dynamic-to-variational amplification rises sharply, and the collapse boundary beta_c is pushed far above its variational scale. On the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at beta_c = 0.224 while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior collapses at 0.00316, a 71x gap from the same pipeline.
  We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d_min/(2 sigma_0), and verify the causal chain through controlled interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995x, 95% CI [0.79, 1.25]). A three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution, bounded anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no amount of RL capacity recovers. The remedy is conditional: a non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would fall into overlap and the task is coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton supports the KL pricing structure - a divergent compactness tax under a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture - and the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource from what requires changing the prior.

Machine Learning.title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a learner-free swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
Machine Learning.summary: The explore/exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum - the ideal-free / Nash allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) - with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium - it stays measurably exploitable - reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 -> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward-free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re-settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two-sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward-free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised-critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74-75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps - its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero-shot, reward-free operating point: a demonstration that the self-organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.

Machine Learning.title: Physics is the Best Teacher: Consistency Learning for Time-Invariant Operators of Chaotic Dynamics
Machine Learning.summary: Accelerating the prediction of long-term behavior in chaotic systems is crucial in scientific computing. However, existing methods rely on numerical solvers or autoregressive models that advance one small step at a time, which makes long horizons expensive. We instead view this problem as learning the system's time-invariant evolution operator, which jumps the state across a large time span in a single evaluation. To this end, we derive the consistency equations a time-invariant operator must satisfy, with differential and compositional objectives in physical time. These equations also connect the learned operator to the physics-prescribed instant dynamics, enabling physics embedding in consistency learning. Across five chaotic systems, we find that physics-distilled consistency makes both short-term trajectories and long-term statistics more accurate. The learned operator survives temporal extrapolation and requires one-tenth as many evaluations as autoregressive rollout, offering an efficient route to long-term simulation of chaotic dynamics.
Machine Learning.comment: 23 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Accepted for the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Stochastic Dynamics

Machine Learning.title: KIRA: A Full-Stack Reading Screening System with Dual-Pathway Analysis for Children
Machine Learning.summary: Early-grade reading screening is critical for identifying children at risk of reading difficulty. Existing AI-based screeners are often limited in the scope of their analyses and evaluation metrics, or are proprietary systems that lack transparent model specifications and evaluation. We present KIRA, a dual-pathway screening system that pairs word-level fluency scoring with detailed phoneme-level error detection. We adapt pretrained word and phoneme recognizers to children's speech, reducing word error rate from 13.88% to 8.84% and phoneme error rate from 41.66% to 23.00%. Powered by these child-adapted models, we implement Word Reading (WRE) and Oral Reading Fluency (ORF), two foundational tasks in K-2 screening. The system integrates these recognizers with a web-based teacher-facing interface presenting fluency scores alongside phoneme feedback for potential targeted intervention. KIRA brings modern child-speech recognition into a full-stack, deployable, classroom-ready reading screener.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to IEEE Spoken Language Technology 2026

Machine Learning.title: Sketch2Sim: an end-to-end modular framework for hand-drawn circuit analysis
Machine Learning.summary: This study proposes a sketch-to-simulation system to solve handwritten circuit diagrams. The system converts raw images into a Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE)-compatible netlist and automatically calculates the circuit's nodal voltages and currents. Another objective is to propose a holistic framework that benefits students and educators by enhancing the teaching and learning experience of electric circuits and expediting engineering design reviews. This article presents a multistage pipeline that converts raw photographs of handwritten electric circuits into executable SPICE-like netlists, providing a solution. A dataset of 1,000 hand-drawn Resistor-Inductor-Capacitor (RLC) circuits was curated and annotated for components, text regions, and character recognition. The proposed system decomposes a circuit diagram into three stages: (i) dual You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detectors for components and text regions, (ii) a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR)-based domain-aware symbol value extraction, and (iii) image processing with thresholding, skeletonization, and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to automatically identify nodes and map them with corresponding components. The proposed system produces the netlist and solves the circuit. The qualitative and quantitative ablation studies on modular stages, as well as end-to-end tests, demonstrate robust performance across various handwriting styles, lighting conditions, and clutter.This study serves as an interactive learning aid and practical tool for professionals, providing a comprehensive user interface (UI), enabling rapid digitization of circuit sketches for study, design, prototyping, or troubleshooting.

Machine Learning.title: SYNAPSE: Framework for Neuron Analysis and Perturbation in Sequence Encoding
Machine Learning.summary: In recent years, Artificial Intelligence has become a powerful partner for complex tasks such as data analysis, prediction, and problem-solving, yet its lack of transparency raises concerns about its reliability. In sensitive domains such as healthcare or cybersecurity, ensuring transparency, trustworthiness, and robustness is essential, since the consequences of wrong decisions or successful attacks can be severe. To overcome these limitations, this work proposes SYNAPSE, a systematic, training-free framework (requiring no retraining of the base model) for understanding and stress-testing the internal behavior of Transformer models across domains. SYNAPSE extracts per-layer [CLS] representations, trains a lightweight linear probe to obtain global and per-class neuron rankings, and applies forward-hook interventions during inference. This design enables controlled, repeatable experiments on internal representations without altering the original model, thereby allowing weaknesses, stability patterns, and label-specific sensitivities to be measured and compared directly across tasks and architectures. SYNAPSE reveals a consistent organization of internal representations across the two evaluated domains, in which task-relevant information is encoded in broad, overlapping neuron subsets. This redundancy provides a strong degree of functional stability, while class-wise asymmetries expose heterogeneous specialization patterns and enable fine-grained, label-aware analysis. In contrast, small structured manipulations in weight or logit space are sufficient to redirect predictions, highlighting complementary vulnerability profiles and illustrating how SYNAPSE can guide the development of more robust and interpretable Transformer models.

Machine Learning.title: $μ_0$: A Scalable 3D Interaction-Trace World Model
Machine Learning.summary: World models that capture how actions induce physical change enable scalable robot learning without reliance on embodiment-specific action labels. Pixel-space video models provide broad visual priors but expend model capacity on dense appearance reconstruction, while direct action models require embodiment-specific labels that hinder scalability. We present $μ_0$, a scalable world model based on 3D traces. Rather than predicting dense pixels or directly modeling actions, $μ_0$ forecasts smooth 3D trajectories for salient interaction points such as objects, tools, hands, and contact regions, yielding a compact, embodiment-agnostic motion interface. To enable training from diverse video sources, our TraceExtract system automatically extracts 3D supervision by selecting keypoints, constructing globally aligned traces, and associating motion segments with hierarchical language captions. This TraceExtract supervision pretrains $μ_0$ by combining a pretrained vision-language backbone with a modular trace expert, which represents each query via B-spline control points and predicts future traces. Experiments show that $μ_0$ outperforms baselines in both 2D and 3D trace prediction, including trace prediction models and tokenized VLM methods. Because $μ_0$ is frozen and reusable, it can be paired with action experts for downstream robot embodiments. Despite action-free pretraining, the resulting trace-conditioned policies achieve performance competitive with VLA models pretrained with action supervision, such as $π_0$. These results establish 3D traces as a scalable and transferable representation for cross-embodiment manipulation.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: Accepted to CoRL 2026. Project Page: https://mu0-wm.github.io/

Machine Learning.title: Brittle by Design? Multi-Scenario Reinforcement Learning for Robust Mission Coordination in Systems of Systems
Machine Learning.summary: As systems engineering (SE) shifts from monolithic systems to Systems of Systems, Mission Engineering (ME) has emerged as a new line of thinking in SE. Mission environments are uncertain and dynamic, and outcomes depend on how mission assets interact with them, rendering static architectures brittle and calling for flexible yet analytically rigorous ME approaches. We propose an intelligent mission coordination methodology integrating high-fidelity digital mission models with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for adaptive task allocation. Using a Digital Engineering (DE) infrastructure comprising a digital mission model and agent-based simulation, we formulate mission tactics management as a Markov Decision Process and train an RL coordinator with Proximal Policy Optimization to map mission states to tactical actions from realized outcomes. An aerial firefighting mission with three scenarios demonstrates the approach. First, all trained coordinators significantly outperform random and heuristic baselines. Second, single-scenario coordinators can be brittle: the coordinator trained on the more forgiving scenario degrades to random tactics performance in more demanding scenarios, whereas the demanding-scenario coordinator retains most of its advantage when transferred. Third, within the same training budget, a coordinator trained on both scenarios concurrently matches the scenario-specific coordinators in their own scenarios and significantly outperforms every other policy. Sensitivity analyses on ignition location, weather, scenario, and training curricula show that the variability represented during training shapes post-deployment performance. This proof of concept shows DE-enabled mission simulations combined with RL offer a reusable methodology for improving ME practice, which can be extended to fleet design and selection from a mission-first perspective.

Machine Learning.title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems
Machine Learning.summary: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.

Machine Learning.title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
Machine Learning.summary: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.

Machine Learning.title: Towards Realistic Models of Change: A Causal Perspective on Decision-Making and Dynamical Systems
Machine Learning.summary:
While statistical learning has made remarkable progress in recent decades, driven by large datasets and data-driven protocols that have transformed scientific practice, it still faces a key limitation: it struggles to generalize beyond the data it has seen, often failing under distribution shift. Causality offers a promising solution: causal models focus on the underlying mechanisms of change rather than surface-level associations, enabling robust reasoning under external interventions.
